claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by lattice-distortion mechanisms arising from atomic-size mismatch.
Lattice distortions caused by atomic-size mismatch act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Alloys with larger atomic-size variation should have proportionally greater hardness and strength than alloys with smaller atomic-size differences.
Atomic-size mismatch can be varied through composition while phase structure and processing history are held as constant as possible.
The controlled comparison should use identical processing conditions and standardized room-temperature nanoindentation and uniaxial mechanical tests.
The proposed relationship applies within a homogeneous, single-phase regime.
The proposed relationship applies at temperatures and strain rates where thermal softening and dynamic recovery do not dominate.
Lattice distortion can be quantified using X-ray diffraction peak broadening and strain analysis.
Transmission electron microscopy can characterize local lattice distortions.
Atomic-size differences induce local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions create barriers to dislocation movement.
Impeded dislocation movement increases yield strength and hardness.
The proposed mechanism resembles solid-solution strengthening but is amplified by high compositional complexity.
Alloys engineered for greater atomic-size mismatch and measured lattice distortion will exhibit significantly higher hardness and yield strength than a minimum-mismatch baseline.
Hardness and yield-strength improvements will scale with the degree of atomic-size mismatch or lattice distortion.
A composition selected to minimize constituent atomic-size differences should have lower intrinsic lattice distortion and can serve as the baseline.
The proposed relationship may fail in multiphase or strongly segregated systems.
The proposed relationship may fail when temperature or strain rate activates different deformation mechanisms.
Local chemical ordering may contribute to strengthening independently of or alongside lattice distortion.

Failure to observe a consistent, statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength at higher measured mismatch and distortion would falsify the claim that lattice distortion is the primary strengthening mechanism.
